court: Office of Hearings and Appeals — Director's Decisions (U.S. Dept. of the Interior)
title: 38 OHA 68 — IN RE NAYLOR
text:
January 29, 2009
IN THE MATTER OF ) Docket No. D 2008-10
LAIRD P. NAYLOR )
) Waiver Request
)
) Waiver Request Granted
ORDER
On November 6, 2007, Sue Bylsma, Supervisor, Taxes and Collections Group,
Payroll Operations Division (POD), National Business Center, Office of the Secretary,
Denver, Colorado, filed with the Office of Hearings and Appeals (OHA) a request for
waiver of salary overpayments submitted by Laird P. Naylor, an employee of the
Bureau of Land Management (BLM), in the total amount of $12,332.92, Bill for
Collection No. M0723200005 (for $10,768.01) and Bill for Collection No.
71980065479 (for $1,564.91).
The record shows that the overpayment was discovered in June 2007, and
Laird P. Naylor was notified of its existence in June 2007. POD prepared an
Administrative Report which accompanied Mr. Naylor’s request and explained the
circumstances of the salary overpayment as follows:
Mr. Laird Naylor, an employee of the Bureau of Land
Management (BLM), received erroneous overpayments of salary due to
the miscoding of his FLSA Class. A personnel action was processed
correcting employee’s FLSA status from non-exempt to exempt. This
correction reduced Mr. Naylor’s overtime rate, which should have been
capped at the GS-10, Step 1 pay.
Administrative Report, RA200700191, at 1.
POD included a summary of the statement of the office involved as follows:
The BLM Human Resources Office submitted a statement stating
that Mr. Naylor was reassigned from [the] National Park Service to
38 OHA 68

D 2008-10
[the] Bureau of Land Management on March 28, 1999 and all SF-50’s
were erroneously coded to non-exempt dated up until January 7, 2007.
BLM further states that Mr. Naylor was unaware of the error
until he was informed by them in June of 2007. Mr. Naylor was not
provided with documents which if reviewed would have alerted him to
the fact that an error had occurred.
Id. at 2.
POD provided the following findings and conclusions regarding Mr. Laird’s
request for waiver:
Waivers of claims for overpayment of wages may be granted
under 5 U.S.C. 5584, when collection would be against equity and good
conscience and not in the best interests of the United States, unless
there is indication of fraud, misrepresentation, fault, or lack of good
faith on the employee’s part. We find no indication of the above in this
matter.
The Comptroller General has consistently held that an employee
is not entitled to a waiver as a matter of legal right whenever they
receive an overpayment through an administrative error. Instead, the
standards implementing the waiver statute state, in general, waiver is
precluded when an employee receives a significant unexplained
increase in pay or allowances, or otherwise knows, or reasonably
should know, that an erroneous payment has occurred and fails to
make inquiries or bring the matter to the attention of the appropriate
officials.
The issue in this case is whether Mr. Naylor can be said to be at
"fault" in this matter as that term is used in the statute. Ordinarily, fault
may be imputed to an employee if there is anything in the record
sufficient to indicate that employee knew or should have known about
the overpayment and failed to question it. In deciding this, we ask
whether a reasonable person in the employee's position should have
been aware that they were receiving more salary payment than they
were entitled to. If so, the employee had the obligation to set aside the
overpayment and hold it for repayment to the Government when the
error was corrected. (CG Decision No. B-259124, Feb. 23, 1995).
38 OHA 69

D 2008-10
We find that in this case, there is nothing in the record to
indicate that the employee knew or should have known that an error
had occurred. Mr. Naylor’s pay and personnel records would not have
alerted him to the fact that an error had occurred. Generally, where an
employee has documentary records, such as SF-50 (Notification of
Personnel Action) and L&E (Leave and Earnings) statements, and fails
to review those documents for accuracy or otherwise fails to take
corrective action, he is not without fault and waiver will be denied.
The record in this case indicates that Mr. Naylor’s personnel records
continually displayed that he was a non-exempt employee for FLSA
purposes. Overtime pay and FLSA status are complicated matters and
Mr. Naylor cannot be presumed to have knowledge of the rules and
regulations governing their applicability to him.
CG Decision No. B-206674 states in general, that waiver of
overpayments is granted where the agency improperly fixed employee’s
rate, and it appeared that the employee was not familiar with the pay
regulations, and was not furnished with pay or personnel records
which, if examined, would have led to the discovery of the error.
Therefore, we do not find Mr. Naylor at fault in this matter and
recommend approval of his request for waiver.
Id. at 2-3.
OHA exercises the Secretary of the Interior’s delegated authority to waive
collection of erroneous payments over $1,500 from employees of the Department of
the Interior and its constituent bureaus. POD has authority to waive debts of less
than $1,500 arising out of erroneous payments under 5 U.S.C. § 5584 (2000). If
POD denies a waiver request, an appeal can be made to this Office.
Pursuant to 5 U.S.C. § 5584 (2000), OHA is authorized to waive claims for
overpayment of pay if collection would be contrary to equity and good conscience
and not in the best interests of the United States. This authority may not be exercised
if there is an indication of fraud, misrepresentation, fault, or lack of good faith by the
employee or any other person having an interest in obtaining a waiver of the claim.
See 344 DM 9. Waiver determinations under 5 U.S.C. § 5584 (2000) are based solely
on the facts and circumstances giving rise to the erroneous payment and the
employee’s knowledge or fault in the matter. See, e.g., In re Fred M. Ritchhart,
18 OHA 47, 49 (1999). In the instant case, it is undisputed that the erroneous salary
overpayments made to Mr. Naylor occurred as the result of administrative error.
38 OHA 70

D 2008-10
It is well settled by decisions of the Comptroller General that where an
employee was aware, or should have been aware, of an overpayment of pay when it
occurred, the employee cannot reasonably expect to retain such payments, but should
set them aside and expect the Government to seek recovery. Additionally, the
employee should make provision for repayment of the overpayments. Bruce C.
Hanson, B-260849, September 19, 1995. In these circumstances, the employee is not
entitled to relief under 5 U.S.C. § 5584 (2000). In such cases, collection of an
overpayment is not considered to be against equity, good conscience, or contrary to
the best interests of the United States. See Joan R. Edwards, B-271616, October 3,
1996; Sandra L. Geer, B-243686, July 2, 1991; L. Mitchell Dick, B-192283,
November 15, 1978.
Waiver is not proper if the employee was aware that he had received an
overpayment. Amadeo Martinez, Jr., B-261628, June 13, 1996. Decisions of the
Comptroller General state that where an agency notifies an employee of an
overpayment, the employee is on notice and precluded from relying on the accuracy
of the overpayment. In such cases, waiver is not appropriate since collection of the
overpayment by the agency would not be against equity and good conscience despite
the absence of fault on the part of the employee. John Wessels, B-265874, May 22,
1996.
As noted by POD, the issue in this case is whether Mr. Naylor can be said to be
at fault in this matter as that term is used in the statute. The standard employed by
the Comptroller General and OHA is to determine whether a reasonable person
should have been aware that he was receiving a payment to which he was not
entitled. Where the reasonable person would have made inquiry, but the employee
did not, then he is not free from fault and the claim cannot be waived. John H.
Young, Jr., B-253640, November 4, 1993.
In this case, Mr. Naylor’s pay and personnel records would not have alerted
him to the fact that an error had occurred. Generally, where an employee has
documentary records, such as Forms SF-50 (Notification of Personnel Action) and
L&E (Leave and Earnings) statements, and fails to review those documents for
accuracy or otherwise fails to take corrective action, he is not without fault and
waiver will be denied. Id.; Gordon Field, M.D., B-224910, June 22, 1987.
Comptroller General decisions have held that if a reasonable person would have
inquired about the correctness of a payment, but the employee did not, then the
employee is not free from fault and the claim may not be waived. Simon B. Guedea,
B-189385, August 10, 1997, and cases cited.
Fault exists if, in light of all the facts, it is determined that an employee
exercising reasonable diligence should have known that an error existed and would
38 OHA 71

D 2008-10
have taken action to see to it that the error was corrected. In re Mary Ann Slim,
18 OHA 57, 58-59 (1999). If so, the employee had the obligation to set aside the
overpayment and hold it for repayment to the Government when the error was
corrected. Anthony Sideris, B-259124, Feb. 23, 1995.
Decisions of the Comptroller General and this Office have held that waiver of
overpayments may be granted where the agency improperly fixed the employee’s pay
rate, and it appeared that the employee was not familiar with the pay regulations,
and was not furnished with pay or personnel records which, if examined, would have
led to the discovery of the error. In this case, the personnel records provided to
Mr. Naylor incorrectly indicated that he was still non-exempt after his promotion.
We find that Mr. Naylor had no reason to believe that his FLSA status was incorrectly
coded. In re Barbara I. Martin, B-206674, March 25, 1982.
In summary, on the basis of the record before us, we find that Mr. Naylor is
without fault in this matter, and that it would be against equity and good conscience
and the best interests of the United States to deny his request for waiver of Bill for
Collection No. M0723200005 (for $10,768.01) and Bill for Collection No.
71980065479 (for $1,564.91) in the total amount of $12,332.92. Accordingly, the
waiver request submitted by Mr. Naylor is hereby granted.
Pursuant to 344 DM 9, this decision constitutes the final administrative
determination by the Department in this matter.
